 (i) Expenses relating to treatment,

(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;

sentences.text: After the Tribunal ascertains the actual extent of permanent disability of the claimant based on the medical evidence, it has to determine whether such permanent disability has affected or will affect his earning capacity.
13. Ascertainment of the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity involves three steps.

The tribunal has to first ascertain what activities of the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of permanent disability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).
The second step is to ascertain his avocation, profession and nature of work before the accident, as also his age.

The third step is to find out whether (I) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii) Whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions so that he continues to earn or can continue to earn his livelihood.

sentences.text: They provide the amount of compensation in cases of this nature would be directly relatable to the percentage of physical disability suffered by the injured vis-a-vis the injuries are specified in the First Schedule of the 1923 Act.
Indisputably where injuries are specified in the First Schedule, the mode and manner provided for the purpose of calculating the amount of compensation would be applicable.

The 1923 Act would also be applicable to the claims applications arising out of the use of motor vehicles in terms of the provisions of the 1988 Act for the purpose of determination of the amount of compensation where the victim of the accident suffers from disability in the cases coming within the purview thereof.

The note appended to the Second Schedule of the 1988 Act raises a legal fiction, stating that "injuries deemed to result in permanent total disablement /

Now, the question arises as to which of the respondent is liable to pay the compensation amount.
The respondent no. 1 is the principal tort feasor being driver and respondent no. 2 is vicariously liable being owner of the offending vehicle.
However, the offending vehicle was insured at the time of accident and the Insurance company has contractual and statutory liability to indemnify the insured.

In the instant case, the insurance company has not been able to prove that any term or condition of insurance policy was breached / violated by the insured in as much as legal offer was filed by the Insurance Company.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Further, in an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the claim petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.
Reference may be made to the judgments titled as New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Sakshi Bhutani & Others., MAC APP. No. 550/2011 decided on 02.07.2012, Bimla Devi & Others v.
Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Others (2009) 13 SC 530, Parmeshwari v. Ammultiirchand Mact No. 1531/16 vs Yaqub Ali (Driver) on 21 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/112056369/
3 & Others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 & Mangla Ram v. Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. & Others 2018, Law Suit (SC) 303.
12.
Thus, an adverse inference is liable to be drawn against him to the effect that the accident in question occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle by him in view of the law laid down in case of Cholamandalam M.S. General Insurance Company Ltd. v. Kamlesh,
2009(3) AD (Delhi) 310.
15.
A conjoint reading of the testimony of the petitioner and documents placed on record in evidence, including the criminal case record (Ex. PW-1/6), which includes certified copy of Charge sheet filed against respondent no. 1, FIR and the site plan MACT No. 1531/16 Dinesh Kumar v.
Yaqub Ali & Anr. Page No. 6 of 20 and medical treatment papers of injured would show that the petitioner received injuries in a Road Traffic Accident.
Moreover, contents of charge sheet is admissible in evidence and deemed to be correct under Rule 7 of Delhi Motor Accident Tribunal Rules, 2008.
There is nothing on record to dispel the inference that petitioner sustained injuries in a road accident which occurred on 07.09.2014 due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle bearing No. DL 2W 2534, being driven by the respondent no. 1.
Also, in the cross-examination of PW-1, I found no such contradiction or inconsistency which could create any doubt upon the veracity of his testimony, accordingly, it stands established that the accident was caused by rash and negligent driving of respondent no. 1 / driver Yaqub Ali, while he was driving the offending vehicle.
This means that the tribunal should consider and decide with reference to the evidence:
(I) Whether the disablement is permanent or temporary;
(ii) if the disablement is permanent, whether it is permanent total disablement or permanent partial disablement;
(iii) If the disablement percentage is expressed with reference to any specific limb,
then the effect of such disablement of the limb on the functioning of the entire body,
that is the permanent disability suffered by the person.
If the Tribunal concludes that there is no permanent disability then there is no question of proceeding further and determining the loss of future earning capacity.
But if the Tribunal concludes that there is MACT No. 1531/16 Dinesh Kumar v. Yaqub Ali & Anr. Page No. 13 of 20 permanent disability then it will proceed to ascertain its extent.
The tribunal has to first ascertain what activities of the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of permanent disability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).
It is not disputed that the functional disability is to be determined as per Schedule I of the Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923 in terms of Section 143 of Motor Vehicles Mact No. 1531/16 vs Yaqub Ali (Driver) on 21 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/112056369/
8 Act.
Indisputably where injuries are specified in the First Schedule, the mode and manner provided for the purpose of calculating the amount of compensation would be applicable.
The 1923 Act would also be applicable to the claims applications arising out of the use of motor vehicles in terms of the provisions of the 1988 Act for the purpose of determination of the amount of compensation where the victim of the accident suffers from disability in the cases coming within the purview thereof.
In fact, permanent disability, therefore, for certain purposes has been co-related with the functional disability.
Disablement and loss of earning capacity are two different aspects and not substitute to each other, however, functional disability, thus, has a direct relationship with the loss of limb.
With 9% permanent MACT No. 1531/16 Dinesh Kumar v. Yaqub Ali & Anr. Page No. 15 of 20 disability in relation to right lower limb and the whole body, considering the percentage of permanent physical disability of the body part involved and the fact that the petitioner was aged about 48 years at the time of accident, I assess the functional disability of petitioner in the present case to be at 5 %.
However, the petitioner being a Government servant has not suffered any financial loss in his salary.
However, compensation which has to be paid must bear some objectives co-relation with the pain and suffering.
The respondent no. 1 is the principal tort feasor being driver and respondent no. 2 is vicariously liable being owner of the offending vehicle.
However, the offending vehicle was insured at the time of accident and the Insurance company has contractual and statutory liability to indemnify the insured.
In the instant case, the insurance company has not been able to prove that any term or condition of insurance policy was breached / violated by the insured in as much as legal offer was filed by the Insurance Company.
